newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ties retailers to goods made in sweatshops.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ties retailers to goods made in sweatshops.

text.p: The U.S. Labor Department said Friday that Sears, Roebuck and Co., Macy's West, Hub Distributing Inc. and Guess were selling clothing and goods manufactured in sweatshops run by Chums Casual of Los Angeles.

In an investigation of Chums, also known as Steven K. Corp., the department found that the company's cutters, sewers and trimmers were paid $170 for 50 to 55 hours of work a week, with the hourly wage averaging as little as $3.10.

The Labor Department, which has been cracking down on sweatshop operations and the retailers who have their garments made there, said it had contacted the retailers in late September after subpoenaing additional sales records from Chums.
Chums has paid $80,000 in back wages to 72 workers and was fined $12,240 for repeat violations of the Fair Labor Standards Act, a federal law aimed at protecting workers.
This was the first time in its "No Sweat" initiative that the Labor Department used a subpoena to obtain records to trace goods from a manufacturer to a retailer.
The department had announced May 20 that Macy's, a unit of Federated Department Stores, J.C. Penney and Specialty Retailers Inc. had also received illegally made goods from Chums.
"It is essential to continue to involve retailers in our efforts to eradicate worker abuse in the garment industry throughout this country," Labor Secretary Robert Reich said in a statement.
"Make no mistake, we will continue to use every tool in our law enforcement arsenal -- including subpoenas-- to trace sweatshop-made goods to retailers," he said.

Reich noted that one of the retailers, Guess, was included on the department's "Fair Labor Fashions Trendsetters List" of 36 retailers and manufacturers that monitor their suppliers to ensure they are not buying garments made in sweatshops.
He said the department was reviewing Guess' monitoring program and would decide after a thorough review whether to remove the company from the list.

Reich has led a major initiative to crack down on sweatshops, beefing up investigations and other enforcement measures. In May he said there were 11,000 sweatshops in the United States, about half the number of cutting and sewing shops in the country.
The Labor Department said Chums had hired an outside firm to monitor its cutting and sewing practices and ensure compliance with federal laws.
